title: 67 Hands on nutritional monitoring of grazing livestock as a teaching tool
content:
Abstract
Hands-on nutritional monitoring of grazing livestock was used to provide real-world data from commercial operations. This data became the foundation for a one-and-a-half-day workshop aimed primarily at women producers. On 3 different ranches owned or operated by women in the Sonora, Texas area we collected a representative composite fecal sample, herbaceous biomass (n = 5, g/0.25 m2), and body condition scores (BCS; 1 to 5 scale) from one group of sheep and goats monthly for 6 months. Fecal samples were analyzed for diet crude protein (CP) and digestible organic matter (DOM) via near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) by the Grazingland Animal Nutrition Laboratory in College Station, Texas. At each collection event, a trained technician collected biological samples and observational data in collaboration with the rancher. Ranchers received diet quality results from the Gan Lab and forage biomass estimates from AgriLife via email after each sampling event. Prior to the workshop, each rancher received a summary of nutritional monitoring results. Sheep diet CP and DOM were 18.98 ± 1.60, 62.58 ± 2.87; 14.95 ± 2.06, 63.27 ± 1.33 and 17.78 ± 0.53, 64.02 ± 1.98 for ranchers A, B, and C respectively. Goat diet CP and DOM were 16.80 ± 1.23, 53.75 ± 6.25; 16.44 ± 1.04, 55.02 ± 2.46 and 16.52 ± 0.91, 52.66 ± 1.71 for ranchers A, B, and C respectively. Sheep BCS were 3.83 ± 0.08, 2.70 ± 0.08, and 2.89 ± 0.1 for ranchers A, B, and C respectively. Goat BCS were 2.95 0.09, 2.81 0.10, and 2.91 0.10 for ranchers A, B, and C respectively. The workshop was held at the Sonora Research Station and consisted of “classroom” discussions on such topics as basic animal nutrition, basic range forage growth and ecology, and climate-smart grazing. Field sessions included low stress livestock handling, body condition scoring, and grazing animal diet selection. Teams of participants competed to select a diet from the pasture that would meet the protein requirement for a specific species/age/sex of animal (e.g. mature lactating nanny, weaned lambs, etc…). Diets selected were analyzed by portable NIRS to provide real-time results. After the field exercises, participants (including ranchers involved in the nutritional monitoring) were presented with the diet CP and DOM results from all 3 ranches followed by a facilitated peer-to-peer discussion. Main topics of discussion were the effects of precipitation and differences between management strategies. The need for more strategic supplemental feeding was a common takeaway. Less experienced participants benefited from exposure to new management techniques and new sources of information, including learning from experienced producers. Experienced producers benefited from peer-to-peer interaction. Post-event evaluation revealed that participants desire future workshops with more written material on topics to be covered in advance.
